terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, deponent; with an accusative, or ut and the subjunctive
evidence: Cic. Fam. 9.24.3: id forīs cēnitandō facillimē cōnsequēre
Traupman 179, 321: aliquid cōnsequī, to get somewhere, to accomplish something
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to obtain, acquire, get, attain, reach”: of reaching what one wanted.

evidence: Tac. Germ. 46.5–6: rem difficillimam adsecūtī sunt
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: with the idea of active exertion, where cōnsequī is rather the attainment of a wish.

evidence: Cic. Sen. 4: quam ut adipīscantur omnēs optant, eandem accūsant adeptam

phrases.latin: cūrā ut valeās; id forīs cēnitandō facillimē cōnsequēre
phrases.english: Look after your health; you’ll achieve that most easily by eating out a lot.

phrases.latin: sēcūrī adversus hominēs, sēcūrī adversus deōs rem difficillimam adsecūtī sunt, ut illīs nē vōtō quidem opus esset
phrases.english: Safe from men, safe from gods, they have achieved the hardest thing of all: they have no need even to pray for anything.

phrases.latin: quam ut adipīscantur omnēs optant, eandem accūsant adeptam
phrases.english: Everyone hopes to reach it, and complains of it once it is reached.

sources: Lewis & Short: consequor · Lewis & Short: assequor · Lewis & Short: adipiscor
